title: Position of the median in an odd-sized ordered list
source: Theory S1-2.3 Quick check 1 (9 ordered values, median is the 5th); new odd sizes
stem: A data set has {N|int} values arranged in order. The median is the \(m\)th value. What is the value of \(m\)?

steps.name: A
steps.text_tex: There are {N|int} values, so the median is in position \(({N|int}+1)/2={A|int}\).
steps.note: A is k+1 and N is 2k+1. Original k=4 gives n=9 and m=5.

title: Median of an even-sized ordered list
source: Theory S1-2.3 Quick check 2 (4th value 10 and 5th value 16, median 13); new even-sum neighbouring values
stem: A data set has 8 values arranged in order. The 4th value is {a|int} and the 5th value is {B|int}. What is the median?

steps.name: A
steps.text_tex: With an even number of values the median is the mid-point of the two middle values: \(({a|int}+{B|int})/2={A|int}\).
steps.note: A is a+d/2 and B is a+d. Original a=10, d=6 gives 5th value 16 and median 13.

title: Cumulative-frequency height at which the median is read
source: Theory S1-2.3 Quick check 3 (n=40, read the median at cf=20); new even sample sizes
stem: A cumulative frequency graph illustrates {N|int} observations. The median is read from the graph at a cumulative frequency of \(k\). What is the value of \(k\)?

steps.name: A
steps.text_tex: The median is read at half of {N|int}, so \(k={A|int}\).
steps.note: A is m and N is 2m. Original m=20 gives n=40 and k=20. (Some texts use (n+1)/2; for a cf graph with large n the conventional reading is n/2.)
